food.text: West African cuisine has roots in ancient history. Yams, native West African rice, millet, sorghum, black-eyed peas and okra were some of the common staples that fed people in the region.

Sedentary farming developed in West Africa among the ancestors of modern West Africans. The Tichitt culture developed in 2200 BCE and lasted until around 200 BCE, part of the long story of settled life in the region.
Farming in Mali included the cultivation of pearl millet, and evidence suggests tillage began as early as the 3rd millennium BCE. That phase ended abruptly around 400 BCE because of a severe drought.
Long before chili peppers arrived from elsewhere, West African cooks flavored food with native spices. These included grains of paradise, grains of Selim, alligator pepper and calabash nutmeg.

Excavation sites such as Kirkissoy near Niamey, Niger (1500–1000 BCE) suggest populations moved southward, bringing agriculture with them. Along with pearl millet, they possibly grew wheat and emmer, grains domesticated much earlier in the eastern Sahara.

Between roughly the 6th century BC and 1st century AD, the western trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and slaves emerged in earnest. Salt, a basic need for any kitchen, was one of the goods that moved across the desert.

Isotopic analysis at early sites in Mali showed that 85% of dietary carbon came from C4 plants, particularly grasses. This indicates people ate either wild cereals such as wild millet or early domesticated species, and it offers some of the earliest evidence of agriculture and cattle herding in West Africa.

By 400 BCE, West Africa had made contact with Mediterranean civilizations, and a regular trade developed. West Africans exported gold, cotton, metal and leather, and received copper, horses, salt, textiles, beads and slaves in exchange. Human beings were part of what came south in the bargain.

At Dhar Néma, in the late period of the Tichitt Tradition, tamed pearl millet was used to temper the tuyeres of an oval-shaped iron furnace, one of 16 on elevated ground. The grain that fed people was also useful in metalworking.

art.text: Nok terracotta sculptures are regarded as the earliest large three-dimensional figurative art in continental Africa, apart from ancient Egypt, and the earliest may date to around 900 BCE. Burial pits at Nok sites held goods such as technically crafted ceramics and numerous stone-beaded necklaces, and some contained materials from organic substances. The soil in the pits was a different colour from the ground around them, and considerable quantities of charcoal were layered among the sculptures. This evidence supports the view that the pits were graves and that the sculptures were part of a complex Nok funerary culture.

The Bura culture of the lower Niger River valley produced terracotta jars used in ritual sacrifice, along with the earliest terracotta equestrian figures found in the Niger River basin. Iron hooked arrowheads were also found alongside these terracotta artifacts.
The Tichitt tradition of Mauritania dates from 2200 to 200 BCE. Its culture included a rock art tradition, numerous funerary tombs, and monumental architecture such as hundreds of tumuli.

The Kintampo culture is known for possibly the earliest figurative art and personal decoration in West Africa, including stone arm bands worn on the body. Clay figurines of dogs, lizards and cows were found at the sites of Boyase hill and Ntersero, before Kintampo rockshelters were abandoned by the second century BCE.
Some Nok terracotta sculptures portray figures wielding slingshots, bows and arrows. This may indicate that Nok people engaged in hunting or trapping wild animals.
One Nok terracotta sculpture depicts two paddling figures together with their goods in a dugout canoe. This may indicate that Nok people used dugout canoes to transport cargo along river tributaries.

Beneath the Bura terracotta jars, archaeologists found beads made of quartzite, nose rings made of brass, and bracelets made from iron or brass. These ornaments lay on human remains placed under the jars.
The Nok clay terracotta tradition is thought to have shaped later West African art traditions. Among these is the Bura culture of Niger, whose own terracotta tradition began in the 3rd century CE.
The Nok culture developed around 1500 BCE in West Africa. It vanished under unknown circumstances around 500 CE.

At Djenné-Djeno in the Niger River Valley, glass beads dating to as early as the third century BCE have been found. They appear to have originated from as far away as Asia and the Mediterranean Near East.
At Dhar Tagant, part of the Tichitt tradition, archaeologists have surveyed approximately 276 tumuli. The site also features various geometric constructions, both rectilinear and circular.

war.text: Soninke oral tradition portrays the early Ghana Empire, known as Wagadu, as very warlike. Horse-mounted warriors were key to increasing its territory and population, though details of this expansion remain scarce.

By 400 BCE, West African smiths were producing both iron tools and weapons through smelting and forging. Around then the region made contact with Mediterranean civilizations, and a regular trade grew up in which West Africa exported gold, cotton, metal and leather in exchange for copper, horses, salt, textiles, beads and slaves. People were part of what was bought and sold in that trade.

By 400 BCE, Mande-speaking Soninke peoples are believed to have built large walled stone settlements at Dhar Tichitt and nearby sites in what is now southeastern Mauritania, dating back to around 1,600 BCE.

Some Nok terracotta sculptures, first made in what is now Nigeria from around 900 BCE, depict figures wielding slingshots, bows and arrows. These weapons may have been used for hunting or trapping undomesticated animals rather than warfare.

Around 250 BCE, the town of Jenné-Jeno in what is now Mali built a large city wall alongside its earliest mudbrick residences. This is considered one of the first known examples of permanent mudbrick architecture, including fortification, in the region.

Iron metallurgy may have developed independently within the Nok culture of what is now Nigeria between 750 BCE and 550 BCE. Nok terracotta art from the same culture also depicts bows, arrows and slingshots, likely used for hunting rather than warfare.

At Djenné-Djeno in the Niger River Valley, the first occupation of the site, known as Phase I, lasted from 250 BCE to 50 CE. This phase produced some of the earliest evidence of iron production found anywhere in West Africa.

science.text: Iron smelting and forging for tools appear in West Africa by 1200 BCE, making it one of the first places where the Iron Age was born. Many Africanists accept that iron use south of the Sahara developed independently.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: The Tichitt culture developed in 2200 BCE and lasted until around 200 BCE. In its late period at Dhar Néma, tamed pearl millet was used to temper the tuyeres of an oval-shaped iron furnace, one of 16 on elevated ground.

Iron remnants and metalworking traces from the 1st millennium BCE turn up across the West African Sahel. Sites include Dhar Tagant, Dia Shoma, Walaldé, Bou Khzama and Djiganyai. At Dhar Walata and Dhar Tichitt, copper was also used.
At Bled Initi, near Akreijit, two depictions of ox carts have been estimated to date between 650 BCE and 380 BCE. They match the artistic style of the Dhar Tichitt Early Iconographic Tradition.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: Around 1st millennium BCE, migrations from the northeast brought iron metallurgists from Niger into West Africa. They spread concave matting techniques for ceramics that originated along the Sudano-Tchadian border. Peoples of the Niger Bend combined fishing, herding, agriculture and iron metallurgy.
Nok settlement sites are often found on mountaintops. Iron metallurgy may have developed independently in the Nok culture between 750 BCE and 550 BCE.

Iron metallurgy may have been independently developed in the Nok culture of Nigeria, which may have practiced iron smelting as early as 1000 BCE, with furnaces appearing there by about 550 BCE. Some recent studies place the start of iron metallurgy in Africa between 3000 and 2500 BC.
At Dhar Néma, in the late Tichitt Tradition, metalworkers tempered the tuyeres of an oval-shaped, low shaft iron furnace with tamed pearl millet. It was one of 16 furnaces located on elevated ground.

politics.text: West African iron industry, in both smelting and forging for tools and weapons, emerged as early as 2631 BCE. By 400 BCE contact had been made with Mediterranean civilizations, and regular trade exported gold, cotton, metal and leather in exchange for copper, horses, salt, textiles, beads and slaves. Human beings were thus among the goods bought in this trade.

The Ghana Empire, also called Wagadu, grew out of a much older political landscape. Its ancestor was likely a large collection of proto-Mande agro-pastoralist chiefdoms spread over the western Niger River basin for over a millennium, roughly 1300 BCE to 300 BCE.

Between roughly the 6th century BC and the 1st century AD, the trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and slaves emerged in earnest. By the 3rd to 6th centuries AD it had become a kind of regional super highway, which helped facilitate the rise of West Africa's earliest great empires.

The Ghana Empire may have been established as early as the 3rd century CE. It belonged to the Sahelian kingdoms, which controlled the trade routes across the desert and were quite decentralised, with member cities having a great deal of autonomy.

The Tichitt culture developed in 2200 BCE and lasted until around 200 BCE. By 400 BCE, West Africans had contact with Mediterranean civilizations and regular trade, exporting gold, cotton, metal and leather in exchange for copper, horses, salt, textiles and beads.

Munsun theorized that around 700 BCE Libyco-Berber raiders destroyed the burgeoning proto-Ghana state. Their opening of a trade route north eventually changed the economic calculus from raiding to trade, and the native Soninke reasserted themselves around 300 BCE.
In the first millennium BC, early cities and towns were founded along the middle Niger River. Dia reached its peak around 600 BC, and Djenne-Djenno was founded around 250 BC.

The development of ironworking technology was crucial to the formation of the Ghana Empire. The local Soninke reasserted themselves around 300 BCE, after a new trade route north changed the economy from raiding to trade.

Trade and the development of ironworking technology were crucial in the formation of the Ghana state. Work at Dhar Tichitt, Dhar Nema and Dhar Walata shows that as the desert advanced, local groups moved south into the still well-watered areas of what is now northern Mali.

culture.text: The Nok culture is named after the village of Nok in southern Kaduna State, Nigeria, where its terracotta sculptures were first discovered in 1928. The culture may have emerged in 1500 BCE and persisted until 1 BCE.

Traditional African religions are the oldest belief systems in West Africa and include Akan religion, Yoruba religion, Odinani-Igbo and Serer religion. Many groups blend social and religious rituals so closely that there is usually not much distinction between them.

Nok people may have developed terracotta sculptures as part of a complex funerary culture that may have included practices such as feasting. The earliest Nok terracotta sculptures may date to 900 BCE.
Craftspeople at Gao fashioned carnelian into beads, some dated as early as the third century. These beads were greatly valued in the Sudan and the West African rainforest.

Some Nok terracotta sculptures show figures wielding slingshots, bows and arrows, which may indicate the hunting or trapping of wild animals. Yet no projectile points made of iron or stone have been found at Nok sites.

Carnelian beads made at Gao have been dated as early as the third century. They were greatly valued across the Sudan and the West African rainforest. Slavery was widely practiced within Gao, although it was not a major center of the slave trade compared with Kanem and Wagadu.
One Nok sculpture portrays two paddling individuals with their goods in a dugout canoe. It may indicate that Nok people used dugout canoes to carry cargo along tributaries.
